content.chapter: Chapter 1: A Hospital Ahead of Its Time
objectives: Explain why the Gevher Nesibe Complex is special.
Compare the start of systematic medical training in Kayseri and in Europe.
Say who built the complex, for whom, and what it is today.
Use the oldest … still standing, did not … until, more than … after and serves as.
content.pedagogy: The opening chapter makes a strong claim (the world’s first hospital and medical school together) and supports it with dates. A time line (13th century Kayseri / 16th–17th century Europe / Mahmud II’s school) makes the comparison visible.
priorKnowledge: The words hospital, school and museum.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The complex was built for Gevher Nesibe, not by her.
The Imperial Medical School is Ottoman and came more than 600 years later; it is not the same building.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: the oldest … still standing · did not … until · more than … after · was built by · serves as
Notice (Activity 1): did not appear … until.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite with is used as, a passive and people called.
Likely errors: *the most old · *more than 600 years before (meaning) · *This center built by.
Use (Activity 4): an old building today.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: GEV-her ne-SI-be, KAY-se-ri, gı-yâ-sed-DIN key-hus-REV, ma-KARR-ı u-le-MÂ.
Stress: the-o-RET-i-cal, PRAC-ti-cal, sys-tem-AT-ic, IM-pe-ri-al.
beforeReading: Ask: “Where do doctors learn today? In a classroom, in a hospital, or both?”
duringReading: First reading: Why is the complex special?
Second reading: complete a time line with three dates.
Find who built it and what it is today.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Time line; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: an old building today; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What does “a hospital and a medical school built together” mean?
What does the comparison with Europe show?
Why was Kayseri called ‘Makarr-ı Ulemâ’?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Kayseri” and “A Museum Today” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: still standing, offered, practical training, appear, serves as.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the time line with the dates written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a three-sentence museum label for the complex.

formativeAssessment: Explains why the complex is special.
Compares Kayseri and Europe with dates.
expectedResponses: The Gevher Nesibe Complex is the oldest Anatolian Seljuk hospital still standing and the world’s first hospital and medical school built together. This kind of training did not appear in Europe until the 16th and 17th centuries.
content.transferTask: Describe an old building that is still standing and what it is used as today.
content.teacherReflection: Did the time line make the comparison clear?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “did not … until” and one with “serves as”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains why the complex is special.
Uses did not … until and serves as.

content.chapter: Chapter 2: A Princess and a Commander
objectives: Retell the legend of Gevher Nesibe in the right order.
Explain the causes and results in the story.
Recognize that this part is a legend (“according to a famous story”).
Use according to, allow … to, instead, to + verb and because / so.
content.pedagogy: A sad, human story. A cause-result chain (love → brother against → commander sent away → death in battle → grief and illness → no hospital → early death) helps learners retell it calmly. Make clear that the book presents it as a legend.
priorKnowledge: The words sister, brother and marry.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The text presents the love story as a legend (“According to a famous story”).
Gevher Nesibe was the Sultan’s sister, not his daughter.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: according to · allow + person + to + verb · instead · to + verb (purpose) · because / so · apologize to
Notice (Activity 1): according to a famous story.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite cause and result.
Likely errors: *allow them marry · *For separate · *apologized her.
Use (Activity 4): something good from something sad.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: kı-lıç-ars-LAN the SEC-ond.
Stress: re-LA-tion-ship, tu-ber-cu-LO-sis /tjuːˌbɜːkjəˈloʊsɪs/, a-POL-o-gized.
beforeReading: Ask: “What is a legend? Do you know a legend from your town?”
duringReading: First reading: Who are the people in the story?
Second reading: make a cause-result chain.
Find the words that show it is a legend.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Legend hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–19 Cause-result chain; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: something good from something sad; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did the Sultan send the commander away?
Why did Gevher Nesibe die young?
What did her brother do on her deathbed?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “A Famous Story” and “Kılıçarslan II” when the picture is in place.
Read the sad parts calmly. Focus on the good result in Chapter 3 and 4.
Word Notes: against, relationship, allow, Instead, tuberculosis, apologized to.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chain with the first and last boxes filled.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Retell the legend in five sentences with because, so and instead.

formativeAssessment: Explains one cause and one result.
Uses allow … to and to + verb correctly.
expectedResponses: According to a famous story, Gevher Nesibe loved a young commander, but her brother did not allow them to marry. To separate them, he sent the commander to war. The commander died, she fell ill, and because there was no good hospital, she died young.
content.transferTask: Describe how something good can come from a sad event.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners retell the story calmly and see it as a legend?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “did not allow … to” and one with “To + verb, …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains a cause and a result.
Uses allow … to and to + verb.

content.chapter: Chapter 3: The Last Wish
objectives: Explain what Gevher Nesibe asked for in her last wish.
Identify the purposes of the hospital and the idea of free charity.
Report her wish in indirect speech.
Use Let + noun + verb, should and has been able to.
content.pedagogy: A short, powerful text in the first person. It turns the sad story into a plan for others. The two-part chart (what the hospital should do / how it should be paid for) shows the idea of a charitable foundation (vakıf).
priorKnowledge: The words illness, doctor and money.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The text says “As the legend goes”; her words are part of the legend.
She did not want doctors to work for free; she wanted patients not to pay.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: Let + noun + base verb · Let + noun + be + past participle · should · has been able to · reported requests (asked … to)
Notice (Activity 1): Let shows a wish.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then report her wish.
Likely errors: *should to pay · *Let surgeons trained · *asked him use.
Use (Activity 4): a wish for my community.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: re-QUEST, SUR-geons, CHAR-i-ty, TER-ri-ble.
Intonation: read her words slowly and calmly; pause after each “Let …”.
beforeReading: Ask: “If you could build one thing to help people in your town, what would it be?”
duringReading: First reading: What did she ask for?
Second reading: complete the two-part chart.
Find the words that show it is a legend.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–18 Two-part chart; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: a wish for my community; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did she want the hospital to be free?
Why did she ask for doctors to be trained there?
How did a sad event become a gift for others?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “The Last Wish” and “A Free Charity” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: request, cure, to honor my memory, treat, surgeons, charity.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with one item in each group.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write her wish as a short letter in reported speech.

formativeAssessment: Explains the idea of free charity.
expectedResponses: She asked her brother to use all her wealth to build a hospital. She wanted it to treat patients, look for cures and train doctors and surgeons, and she said that nobody should pay any money.
content.transferTask: Write a wish for your community with Let and should.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see how her wish helped other people?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “Let …” and one with “should” about the hospital.

content.chapter: Chapter 4: The Twin Madrasas
objectives: Describe the madrasa and the hospital and why they are called the Twin Madrasas.
Explain how we know the building date (the writing on the gate).
Say where Gevher Nesibe was buried.
Use to + verb for purpose, the passive was buried and according to.
content.pedagogy: A short factual chapter that completes the legend: the wish comes true. A simple plan drawing (two buildings side by side, the tomb in the madrasa, the gate with the date) helps learners remember the facts.
priorKnowledge: The words madrasa, gate and tomb.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The madrasa is the Gıyâsiye and the hospital is the Şifâiye; they are two buildings.
The date comes from the writing on the hospital gate.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: to + verb (purpose) · was buried (passive) · people call them … · according to · last / take (time)
Notice (Activity 1): To follow his sister’s wish.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite with so, took and are called.
Likely errors: *For follow · *She buried in her tomb · *lasted two years to build.
Use (Activity 4): a place with a special name.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: gı-yâ-SI-ye med-re-se-Sİ, şi-fâ-I-ye.
Stress: con-STRUC-tion, MAD-ra-sa, TWIN.
beforeReading: Ask: “What do people call two things that are very similar and next to each other?”
duringReading: First reading: draw the two buildings.
Find the date and where it comes from.
Find where Gevher Nesibe was buried.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading and drawing; 11–17 Facts check; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–34 Language Focus 1–3; 34–42 Use: a place with a special name; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did the Sultan build the two buildings?
Why are they called the Twin Madrasas?
How do we know the date?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “The Twin Madrasas” and “The Main Gate” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: lasted.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the drawing with labels to place.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a sign for visitors to the Twin Madrasas in four sentences.

formativeAssessment: Uses to + verb and was buried.
expectedResponses: To follow his sister’s wish, the Sultan built a madrasa and a hospital. Because they are next to each other, people call them the Twin Madrasas. According to the writing on the gate, the hospital was built in 1205–1206.
content.transferTask: Explain the special name of a place you know.
content.teacherReflection: Did the drawing help learners remember the facts?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “To + verb, …” and one with “according to”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains the name and the date.
Uses to + verb and the passive.

content.chapter: Chapter 5: Learning Beside the Patients
objectives: Explain how theory (Gıyâsiye) and practice (Şifâiye) were combined.
Describe the heating, the rooms, the courtyards and the staff.
Separate facts from guesses in the text.
Use probably, historians think, we do not know for sure, were held and similar to.
content.pedagogy: This chapter is a good place to teach how history writers show certainty. A two-column chart (fact / guess) makes learners read carefully and copy the writer’s honest language in their own writing.
priorKnowledge: The words doctor, surgeon and pharmacist.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The number of doctors is a guess (“historians think”), not a fact.
The heating used steam from a bathhouse; it was not a fire in the rooms.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: probably · we do not know for sure · historians think · historical studies show · were held (passive) · similar to
Notice (Activity 1): fact or guess?
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then show certainty with may/might and think.
Likely errors: *classes held · *similar with · *Students probably were live.
Use (Activity 4): learning by doing.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: key-kâ-VUS, si-VAS.
Stress: the-O-ry, PHAR-ma-cist, AS-sis-tants, SPA-cious, OUT-pa-tients.
beforeReading: Ask: “Can you learn to be a doctor only from books? Why or why not?”
duringReading: First reading: Where did students learn theory and practice?
Second reading: complete the fact / guess chart.
Find the people who worked there.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–19 Fact / guess chart; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: learning by doing; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why is learning beside patients useful?
How was the building heated?
Which sentences are guesses? How do you know?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Underfloor Heating” and “The Staff” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: nearby, inside, staff, similar to.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the fact / guess chart with the signal words highlighted.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short paragraph about the staff using think, probably and similar to.

expectedResponses: Students learned theory at the Gıyâsiye and practiced at the Şifâiye. Students probably lived inside the complex, and historians think the staff had a chief doctor, two general doctors, two surgeons and a pharmacist.
content.transferTask: Describe something you learned by doing it.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners notice the difference between facts and guesses?

exitTicket: Write one fact and one guess about the hospital. Use “probably” in the guess.

content.chapter: Chapter 6: Great Teachers and Books
objectives: Name the teachers of the institution and say what they were known for.
List the subjects taught at the Gıyâsiye and the books students read.
Explain where practical training took place.
Use non-defining who-clauses, some of them and especially.
content.pedagogy: A chapter full of names. A “who’s who” card set (name / known for) and a book shelf drawing (er-Râzî, İbn Sînâ, Hippocrates, Galen) organize the information. Who-clauses are the natural grammar for introducing people.
priorKnowledge: The names Mevlânâ and İbn Sînâ.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Hippocrates and Galen did not teach there; students read Arabic translations of their books.
Practical training was at the Şifâiye, not at the Gıyâsiye.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: non-defining who-clause · some of them · especially · take place · on the other hand
Notice (Activity 1): who was a famous eye doctor.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then join sentences with who.
Likely errors: *some of they · *was taken place · *, that was a famous doctor.
Use (Activity 4): a teacher who inspired me.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: sad-red-DIN ko-ne-VÎ, ek-me-led-DIN al-nah-çu-VÂ-nî, kut-büd-DIN eş-şî-RÂ-zî, er-RÂ-zî, ibn SÎ-nâ, hip-POC-ra-tes, GA-len.
Stress: in-sti-TU-tion, PHI-los-o-phy, AN-cient.
beforeReading: Ask: “Who are famous doctors or scientists from our history?”
duringReading: First reading: list the teachers.
Second reading: complete the who’s who cards.
Find the subjects and the books.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–19 Who’s who cards; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: a teacher who inspired me; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why was it important to have famous teachers?
Which subjects did students learn at the Gıyâsiye?
Where did practical training take place?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Great Teachers” and “Important Books” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: institution, era.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the cards with the names; learners add the descriptions.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short “Who’s who” paragraph with three who-clauses.

expectedResponses: Some of the teachers were Sadreddin Konevî and Ekmeleddin al-Nahcuvânî, who was Mevlânâ’s close friend and doctor. Students studied the medical books of the era, especially the works of er-Râzî and İbn Sînâ.
content.transferTask: Describe a teacher who inspired you.
content.teacherReflection: Did the cards make the many names easier?

exitTicket: Write one sentence about a teacher in this chapter with a who-clause.

rubricLevels.secure: Names teachers and what they were known for.

content.chapter: Chapter 7: Inside the Buildings
objectives: Describe the inside of the madrasa and the hospital.
Explain what the evidence shows (no kitchen, small windows, no chimneys).
Describe the operating rooms and the work done there.
Use none of, each one has, this shows that and which made it easier to.
content.pedagogy: The chapter reads a building like a detective: details become evidence for conclusions. A two-column chart (detail / what it shows) develops reasoning in simple English.
priorKnowledge: The words room, door and window.
anticipatedMisconceptions: There was no kitchen inside; food came from an outdoor kitchen.
The surgeries were minor operations and cataract operations, according to “probably”.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: none of + plural · each one + singular verb · this shows that · which made it easier to · probably
Notice (Activity 1): this shows that.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then connect evidence and conclusion.
Likely errors: *each one have · *No of the rooms · *, what made it easier.
Use (Activity 4): a building detective.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: COR-ri-dor, COURT-yard, CHIM-neys, OP-er-at-ing, CAT-a-ract.
beforeReading: Ask: “If a house has no kitchen, what can you guess about it?”
duringReading: First reading: list the parts of the buildings.
Second reading: complete the detail / what it shows chart.
Find the work done in the operating rooms.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–19 Detective chart; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: a building detective; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What does the missing kitchen show?
Why were the windows in the operating rooms small?
Why do you think there were no chimneys?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Operating Rooms” and “Dim Light” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: courtyard, chimneys, operating rooms, dim light.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the detective chart with the details written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short tour of the hospital for visitors with three pieces of evidence.

formativeAssessment: Uses none of and this shows that.
expectedResponses: There was no kitchen inside the center, which shows that meals came from an outdoor kitchen. Small windows at the top of the operating rooms gave dim light, which made it easier to control the light during operations.
content.transferTask: Explain what the details of a building tell you.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners connect details with conclusions?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “This shows that” about the hospital.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses none of and this shows that.

content.chapter: Chapter 8: Caring for Mind and Body
objectives: Describe the mental health section (18 rooms) and the openings in the walls.
Explain the use of music and suggestion therapy.
Describe the bathhouse and its sewage system.
Use each, use … for / to and there is / there are.
content.pedagogy: A short descriptive chapter that shows care for both mind and body. A simple floor plan (nine rooms on each side, openings in the walls) and a list of features of the bathhouse support the description.
priorKnowledge: The words mind, body and bath.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The openings carried sound for therapy; the text does not say they were for light.
The bathhouse is inside the building.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: each + singular · use … for + noun / to + verb · there is / there are · also
Notice (Activity 1): used them for.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite the purpose.
Likely errors: *Each rooms · *There is four windows · *used them for play.
Use (Activity 4): a place that calms the mind.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: MEN-tal, SUG-ges-tion /səɡˈdʒestʃən/, THER-a-py, SEW-age /ˈsuːɪdʒ/.
beforeReading: Ask: “What can help a person who feels stressed or sad?”
duringReading: First reading: draw the mental health section.
Find how the openings were used.
Second reading: list the features of the bathhouse.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading and plan; 11–17 Bathhouse features; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–34 Language Focus 1–3; 34–42 Use: a place that calms the mind; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why do you think the hospital had a section for mental health?
How can music help patients?
Why was a good sewage system important?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Rooms for the Mind” and “The Bathhouse” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: experts, suggestion therapy, sewage system.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the floor plan with labels.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short paragraph: “Caring for mind and body at the hospital.”

formativeAssessment: Uses there is / there are correctly.
expectedResponses: The center had 18 rooms for mental health patients. Each room had two small openings that carried sound, and experts used them for music and suggestion therapy. There is also a bathhouse with a dome and a good sewage system.
content.transferTask: Describe a place that helps people feel calm.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see the care for both mind and body?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “used … for” and one with “there are”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses there is / are and each.

content.chapter: Chapter 9: Medical Education at the Dârüşşifâ
objectives: Describe the master-apprentice model and the icâzet.
Explain the two stages of education.
Explain how treatment, medicines and bedside learning worked.
Use was based on, students who …, continue to and known as.
content.pedagogy: A chapter about how education worked. A diagram of the icâzet (student → teacher → teacher’s teacher) shows the “line of tradition”, and a two-stage chart sorts the subjects.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The icâzet listed teachers in a line of tradition; it was not a list of subjects.
The hospital worked until the early 20th century, not only in the Seljuk period.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: be based on · defining who-clause · continue to + verb · be known as · by + -ing
Notice (Activity 1): was based on.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then change active and passive.
Likely errors: *based in · *continued provide · *known like.
Use (Activity 4): learning from a master.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: i-CÂ-zet, dâ-niş-MEND, dâ-rü’l-İ-lim, bî-RÛ-nî.
Stress: AP-pren-tice /əˈprentɪs/, as-TRON-o-my, OB-serv-ing.
beforeReading: Ask: “How do people learn a craft, such as carpentry or cooking, from a master?”
duringReading: First reading: What was the icâzet?
Second reading: complete the two-stage chart.
Find how long the hospital worked.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–19 Icâzet diagram and stages; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: learning from a master; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did the icâzet list the teachers?
Why did students observe doctors at patients’ bedsides?
What does it tell us that the hospital worked for about 700 years?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “The Icâzet” and “Until the 20th Century” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: master-apprentice model, Treatment, observing, provide.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the stage chart with the headings.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short paragraph comparing education then and now.

formativeAssessment: Sorts the subjects into two stages.
Uses was based on and continued to.
expectedResponses: Education was based on the master-apprentice model. Students who graduated received an icâzet. The first stage included mathematics, astronomy, physics, languages, philosophy and medicine; in the second stage, students learned Islamic sciences.
content.transferTask: Describe learning a skill from an expert.
content.teacherReflection: Did the icâzet diagram make the “line of tradition” clear?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “was based on” and one with “Students who …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses was based on and who-clauses.

content.chapter: Chapter 10: Music Therapy at the Dârüşşifâ
objectives: Explain what İbn Sînâ, Er-Râzî and Fârâbî said about music and healing.
Explain how Fârâbî grouped musical modes.
Separate reported ideas from the writer’s conclusion.
Use stated that, believed that, noted that and it is clear that.
content.pedagogy: A chapter of reported ideas. A three-column chart (scholar / idea / reporting verb) helps learners report correctly, and the last sentence models a conclusion based on evidence.
priorKnowledge: The names İbn Sînâ and Fârâbî.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The text does not say music cured every illness; it says it can help patients heal.
“It is clear that” is the writer’s conclusion, not a scholar’s words.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: stated / believed / noted that · reported speech · based on · It is clear that
Notice (Activity 1): reporting verbs vs the writer’s conclusion.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose that / can / on, then report direct speech.
Likely errors: *stated what · *based in feelings · *believed music cans.
Use (Activity 4): music and feelings.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: ki-TÂ-bü’ş-şi-FÂ, er-RÂ-zî, fâ-RÂ-bî, ma-KAM.
Stress: av-i-CEN-na, MU-si-cal, THER-a-py.
beforeReading: Play a short calm piece and a short fast piece. Ask: “How did each one make you feel?”
duringReading: First reading: list the three scholars.
Second reading: complete the scholar / idea chart.
Find the writer’s conclusion.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Music hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–19 Scholar chart; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: music and feelings; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: How can stronger minds help patients?
What did Fârâbî explain about times of the day?
Why does the writer say it is clear that music therapy was used?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “İbn Sînâ” and “Fârâbî and the Makams” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: spirits, courage, heal.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with the reporting verbs written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short report of the three scholars’ ideas with three different reporting verbs.

expectedResponses: İbn Sînâ stated that making patients’ minds and spirits stronger helps them heal. Er-Râzî noted that doctors should treat sad patients with music, and Fârâbî studied how musical modes affect the soul.
content.transferTask: Explain how music affects feelings, with a reported idea.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners report the scholars’ ideas correctly?

exitTicket: Write one sentence reporting a scholar’s idea with “believed that”.

rubricLevels.notYet: Point to It is clear that.

content.chapter: Chapter 11: A Legacy That Lives On
objectives: Explain why the Gevher Nesibe Hospital is unique in history.
Compare it with Salerno, Bologna and Paris.
Explain how Gevher Nesibe “lived on” after her death.
Use none of them, more advanced, compare it to and but.
content.pedagogy: The closing chapter brings the book together: a unique building, a comparison with Europe and the human story. The museum guide project lets learners revisit every chapter.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The text says the hospital was more advanced “in many ways”, not in every way.
Gevher Nesibe lived on in people’s hearts and memory, not literally.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: none of them · more + adjective · compare it to · but (contrast) · live on
Notice (Activity 1): never …, but ….
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then summarize with like, than and continued.
Likely errors: *No of them · *more advanced that · *compare it than.
Use (Activity 4): a legacy for the future.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: sa-LER-no, bo-LO-gna, PAR-is.
Stress: ad-VANCED, col-LEC-tive, LEG-a-cy.

metadata.title: The Gevher Nesibe Hospital B1 — Teacher’s Book
metadata.subtitle: The Gevher Nesibe Hospital and Medical School (Gevher Nesibe Dârüşşifâsı ve Tıp Medresesi)
metadata.estimatedDuration: 11 chapter units of 45 minutes each. Whole-book review pages follow separately.
metadata.targetLearners: Learners who can follow connected texts about history, buildings and science, and who can produce supported explanations and short reflections.
metadata.purpose: Develop evidence-based B1 reading, listening, speaking and writing through the story of the Gevher Nesibe Hospital in Kayseri: the legend, the buildings, medical education and music therapy, using the Language Focus attached to every story chapter.
metadata.approachDesc: Every story chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading establish meaning and evidence; the Quick Challenge checks comprehension. Grammar is then learned inductively: in the Language Focus, learners first NOTICE a form in a real chapter sentence and work out what it does, then BUILD it in controlled, meaningful practice, and finally USE it in connected YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own world. The book also shows learners how a writer separates facts, guesses and legends.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 11 Quick Challenges, text-evidence checks, chapter Language Focus tasks (Notice → Build → Use), exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review and Final Challenge.

formative: Short spoken and written Use tasks

readingFramework.before: Activate only what the chapter needs: a short question, a picture or a plan of the building.
readingFramework.during: Listen first for gist (when the audio is ready), then read and follow the chapter’s own structure: legend, cause and result, description, evidence and conclusion, or reported ideas.
readingFramework.after: Complete the Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (notice → build → use), then a connected B1 transfer about the learners’ own world.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Word Notes are the bold words of the teacher-approved text. Prioritize them and the words needed for the chapter’s key idea.
vocabularyApproach.method: Infer meaning from context, a picture or a plan before any direct explanation.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse vocabulary in Language Focus production, exit tickets and the cumulative review.

metadata.grammarApproach: Inductive and text-based. Start from the story sentence, ask a meaning question (What does this form tell us?), let learners formulate the rule in their own words, then confirm it and practice it in context. Rule explanations appear in the app only after learners answer.
grammarSequence: Ch1: the oldest … still standing · did not … until · more than … after · was built by · serves as
Ch2: according to · allow + person + to + verb · instead · to + verb (purpose) · because / so · apologize to
Ch3: Let + noun + base verb · Let + noun + be + past participle · should · has been able to · reported requests (asked … to)
Ch4: to + verb (purpose) · was buried (passive) · people call them … · according to · last / take (time)
Ch5: probably · we do not know for sure · historians think · historical studies show · were held (passive) · similar to
Ch6: non-defining who-clause · some of them · especially · take place · on the other hand
Ch7: none of + plural · each one + singular verb · this shows that · which made it easier to · probably
Ch8: each + singular · use … for + noun / to + verb · there is / there are · also
Ch9: be based on · defining who-clause · continue to + verb · be known as · by + -ing
Ch10: stated / believed / noted that · reported speech · based on · It is clear that
Ch11: none of them · more + adjective · compare it to · but (contrast) · live on

skillsFocus.listening: TYMM YDAB1: follow narration for gist, people, places and key details.
skillsFocus.reading: TYMM YDAB2: identify main ideas, evidence, legend and fact, cause and result, and reported ideas.
skillsFocus.speaking: TYMM YDAB3: describe places and people, explain causes and purposes, and report ideas respectfully.
skillsFocus.writing: TYMM YDAB4: produce connected B1 paragraphs using evidence, linking words and chapter patterns.

valuesFocus: D9 Compassion — Care for sick people and for the mind as well as the body.
D16 Responsibility — Keeping a promise and serving the community.
D3 Diligence — Hard work in learning and in medicine.
D14 Respect — Respect for teachers, scholars and patients.
languageFocus: Every one of the 11 chapters has a Language Focus set built as Notice → Build → Use (4 activities).
Use the Language Focus after basic comprehension and the Quick Challenge.
Always start from the story sentence and ask a meaning question before naming the form.
The Use step is connected spoken or written production about a new, non-story situation.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Reduce linguistic load without lowering the reasoning target: one paragraph at a time, charts given in part, selected vocabulary, audio replay, sentence frames and oral rehearsal. Extend by combining more chapter patterns or adding a second piece of evidence, not by introducing outside facts.

sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful teaching
notes: Keep explanations within the wording of the book; do not add outside details or opinions.

Chapters 2 and 3 are presented as a legend (“According to a famous story”, “As the legend goes”). Read them calmly; the death of the commander and of Gevher Nesibe are told briefly and should not be dramatized.
Treat mental health respectfully; never use the topic for jokes.
Bracketed Turkish names in the text belong to the teacher-approved story; they are read as they are.

globalCitizenship.title: Global Citizenship and Cultural Bridges
globalCitizenship.description: The Gevher Nesibe Hospital links a Seljuk city with questions every community faces: how to care for the sick, how to train good doctors and how to turn a loss into a gift for others.

themes.title: Health care for everyone:
themes.description: Gevher Nesibe wanted a free hospital (Chapter 3). Discuss how communities today help people who cannot pay for care.

themes.title: Learning by doing:
themes.description: Students learned theory and practice together (Chapters 5 and 9). Compare this with internships and practical training today.

themes.title: Mind and body:
themes.description: The hospital cared for mental health and used music (Chapters 8 and 10). Discuss why mental health matters.

themes.title: Knowledge from many cultures:
themes.description: Students read İbn Sînâ, er-Râzî, Hippocrates and Galen (Chapter 6). Discuss how knowledge travels between cultures.

actions: Find one health or charity organization in your area and write two sentences about what it does.
Make a short poster: “Five ways to look after your mind”.
Interview a nurse, doctor or pharmacist about how they learned their job.

exitTicket: One idea from today’s chapter, with the sentence that supports it, is …
One language pattern I noticed today, and what it does in the sentence, is …
One action I can take this week that shows a value from the chapter is …

miniProject.title: A Museum Guide to the Gevher Nesibe Hospital
miniProject.desc: In groups, choose one part of the book: the legend, the Twin Madrasas, teaching, the buildings, mind and body, education or music therapy. Make a one-page guide in clear English with three facts, one sentence quoted exactly from the book and one reason why it matters today.

reflectivePrompt.title: A Gift for Others
reflectivePrompt.desc: Gevher Nesibe turned her own sad story into a free hospital for many people (Chapters 3 and 11). Write six to eight sentences about a person or a group that helps others in your community. What do they do, and what happens as a result?

valuesEducation.title: TYMM Values in Action
valuesEducation.description: Use only values the chapter really shows. Ask for the sentence first, then connect the value to a small action learners can do and see. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/erdem-deger-eylem-cercevesi.

items.label: D9 Compassion
items.value: Compassion: Gevher Nesibe wanted a free hospital for everyone, and the hospital cared for mind and body (Chapters 3 and 8).

items.label: D16 Responsibility
items.value: Responsibility: The Sultan followed his sister’s wish and built the hospital (Chapter 4).

items.label: D3 Diligence
items.value: Diligence: Students learned from masters and at patients’ bedsides (Chapters 5 and 9).

items.label: D14 Respect
items.value: Respect: Great teachers and scholars were honored and their ideas were used (Chapters 6 and 10).

questions: What small action can show it this week?
Which part is from the book and which part is my own idea?

cefrProfile.intro: This book is written for CEFR B1. The table links the B1 descriptors of the End-of-Level Test B1 to the chapters of this book where learners practice them.

rows.descriptor: Can read straightforward factual texts on subjects related to his/her field and interest with a satisfactory level of comprehension.
practice: Chapter 5 (Learning Beside the Patients): Separate facts from guesses.
Whole book: Knowledge Check and Final Challenge.

rows.descriptor: Can write straightforward connected texts on a range of familiar subjects within his field of interest, by linking a series of shorter discrete elements into a linear sequence.
practice: Chapter 7 (Inside the Buildings): Write what the details of a building tell you.
Chapter 11 (A Legacy That Lives On): Write about something you would like to leave for future generations.
Language Review, “Use: A Place That Helps People”: Write six to eight sentences.

rows.descriptor: Can reasonably fluently sustain a straightforward description of one of a variety of subjects within his/her field of interest, presenting it as a linear sequence of points.
practice: Chapter 2 (A Princess and a Commander): Retell the legend in order.
Chapter 11: Read your page of the class museum guide aloud.

test.title: End-of-Level Test B1
test.when: Give the test when the class has finished the B1 books it reads this term. It has four parts and takes about 70 minutes plus a short speaking test for each learner.
parts: Reading and Language (45 minutes): in the app. The learner gets a test code at the end.
Writing (25 minutes): on paper. Write an article for your school website about a person you admire. (100–130 words)
Speaking (about 8 minutes): one learner with the teacher, in 2 parts.
Scoring: type the test code in “Score a test”, then score Writing and Speaking with the bands. Copy the pilot line for the pilot results sheet.

metadata.title: The Gevher Nesibe Hospital B1 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Read • Find • Check • Build • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 25 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: B1 learners who study the story of the Gevher Nesibe Hospital alone or with a teacher.
learningGoals: Understand the 11 chapters of The Gevher Nesibe Hospital.
Find evidence in the text before answering.
Follow the legend, the buildings and the medical education of the Gevher Nesibe Hospital.
Separate facts, guesses and legends, and explain the legacy of the hospital with evidence.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in connected sentences.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Read (and listen, when the audio is ready) before the Quick Challenge.
Repair wrong answers with the text.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 11.

readingDiary.intro: Keep this diary when you finish the book. Write short answers.
prompts: The date I finished the book:
My favorite chapter, and one reason:
One fact about the Gevher Nesibe Hospital that surprised me:
One sentence for a friend: “Read this book because …”
One new word I want to keep:
The next book I want to read in the library:

sections.title: 1. Make Your Plan
sections.text: This book has 11 chapters. Plan the whole book before Chapter 1.
points: Choose your study days and how many chapters you will read each week.
Write one personal goal for this book.
Save new words to My words and review them after one day, three days and one week.

sections.title: 2. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 25 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and the “Before You Read” question.
Read for the main idea.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 3. Read and Listen
sections.text: Read every chapter twice: once for the main idea, once for the details. When the audio is ready, listen once while you follow the text.
points: First reading: What is the chapter about?
Second reading: Mark names, dates and linking words.
Say one long sentence aloud with the right pauses.

sections.title: 4. Word Notes
sections.text: Bold words have Word Notes. Use them after you have tried to understand the sentence yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Write the word in a new sentence of your own.

sections.title: 5. Quick Challenge
sections.text: Answer before you read the feedback. If you are wrong, repair the answer with the text.
points: Find the paragraph the question is about.
Read the key sentence again.
Explain why the right answer is right, then try again.

sections.title: 6. Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has 4 Language Focus activities built from the chapter’s own sentences.
points: Activity 1 (Notice): Look at a sentence and what it means.
Activities 2–3 (Build): Choose, complete, correct or rewrite forms.
Activity 4 (Use): Write or say connected sentences about a different situation.

sections.title: 7. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Some chapters have many names and dates. Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Read one paragraph only.
Make a time line of the dates.
List the names and what each one did.
Learn only three words today.

sections.title: 8. Values in the Book
sections.text: The book shows compassion, responsibility, diligence and respect. Find the sentence first, then think of a small action of your own.
points: Compassion: Compassion: Gevher Nesibe wanted a free hospital for everyone, and the hospital cared for mind and body (Chapters 3 and 8).
Responsibility: Responsibility: The Sultan followed his sister’s wish and built the hospital (Chapter 4).
Diligence: Diligence: Students learned from masters and at patients’ bedsides (Chapters 5 and 9).
Respect: Respect: Great teachers and scholars were honored and their ideas were used (Chapters 6 and 10).

sections.title: 9. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 11, do the review pages in this order. Go back to a chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Knowledge Check
Vocabulary Challenge
Master Glossary
Language Review
Final Challenge

sections.title: 10. Look Back
sections.text: Before Chapter 1 and again at the end, answer the “I can” statements of a few chapters. What can you do now that you could not do before?
points: Which chapter changed what you knew?
Tell the story of Gevher Nesibe and her hospital in five sentences to someone at home, in your home language or in English.
